newsitem.title: USA: IRS yield burning plan triggers cottage industry. [CORRECTED 22:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: IRS yield burning plan triggers cottage industry. [CORRECTED 22:51 GMT]

text.p: A Minnesota accounting firm has offered to calculate what municipal bond issuers may owe IRS under the Service's recent "yield burning" notice for a fee of $1,000 per issue, a letter obtained by Reuters says.

Barthe & Wahrman (Corrects), based in Bloomington, said in the Sept. 19 three-page letter addressed to issuers nationwide that it is offering an "independent service" to help municipal financial managers grapple with the problem.
"The IRS places the responsibility on you for determining whether yield burning has occurred," the firm's letter says.
Municipalities would have to agree to pay Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest on that figure, IRS said.
Amy Dunbar, director of governmental affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, said her group recently notified about 100 bond lawyers about the Barthe & Wahrman letter via E-Mail.
David Walton, a partner with Jones Hall Hill & White in San Francisco and a former IRS attorney, called Barthe & Wahrman "opportunists."

"IRS is studying the issue. This (letter) assumes that people are going to buckle under and just send IRS a check. I think there are some serious questions on the appropriateness of the IRS standard," including use of the spot price, Walton said.
Walton said the National League of Cities and other groups "need to be very vocal to IRS about putting the burden of all this enforcement on the cities."
"Why should cities have to pay money to these accountants to figure out something that the IRS, if they have a concern, should be looking at" during audits of municipalities, Walton said.

Barthe & Wahrman said it recently examined a refunding bond issue of less than $10 million and calculated "a yield burn in excess of $100,000. Failure to comply with the Revenue Ruling could also result in the loss of the bond issue's tax exempt status," the firm added.
